problem.title: Solving GraphQL N+1 Queries with DataLoader
problem.prompt: A mobile app release adds a `seller { rating }` field to the Order History screen, issuing `orders(first: 50) { id items { qty product { id title seller { id name rating } } } }`. Your Apollo/Java GraphQL Gateway resolves each field independently: 1 query for 50 orders -> 50 queries for items -> 200 queries for products -> 200 gRPC calls for sellers = **451 backend calls per HTTP request**. At just 60 mobile RPS, backend traffic surges to **27,060 QPS**, saturating PostgreSQL and `Seller-Service` and causing 503s. Redesign the GraphQL execution layer to bound backend queries and protect against arbitrary nested queries.
requirements: Reduce backend calls for the 50-order nested query from **451** down to **<= 4** batched calls (1 per entity tier).
Prevent malicious or accidental deep-nested queries (e.g., `order -> items -> product -> seller -> orders -> ...`) from exhausting server CPU/DB.
Ensure `DataLoader` caches are strictly request-scoped so user A never sees user B's data or stale mutations.
Keep GraphQL Order History p99 latency under **120 ms** at 500 RPS.
constraints: GraphQL Gateway runs on Java (`graphql-java` / Netflix DGS) or Node/Python.
Orders and Items live in PostgreSQL; Seller ratings live in `Seller-Service` (gRPC).
Cannot rewrite the mobile app immediately; old mobile clients must be supported cleanly.

stages.learnerPrompt: Why did adding one `seller { rating }` field at 60 RPS generate 27,060 QPS?

referenceMaterial.summary: Unbatched nested resolvers multiply calls at every list level: `1 + 50 + 200 + 200 = 451` calls/req * 60 RPS = 27,060 QPS.
approachSteps: Enable GraphQL tracing / OpenTelemetry spans to count resolver invocations per request.
Identify each list-to-entity fan-out (`orders -> items -> product -> seller`).
tradeOffs: factor: Naive Resolvers vs. DataLoader; pro: Simple to write initially.; con: Exponential DB amplification on nested lists.
alternatives: name: Denormalized Read View; whenToUse: Read-heavy order history.; tradeOff: Duplicates seller rating updates.
failureModes: name: Connection Pool Exhaustion; description: 27,060 QPS exhausts PostgreSQL connections in seconds.; mitigation: Batch via DataLoader.

stages.learnerPrompt: Implement a request-scoped `DataLoader` for `Seller-Service` and configure query depth/complexity limits.

referenceMaterial.summary: Use request-scoped `MappedBatchLoader` for items, products, and sellers, paired with depth <= 6 and complexity <= 500.
tradeOffs: factor: MappedBatchLoader vs. BatchLoader; pro: `MappedBatchLoader` handles missing IDs cleanly without positional alignment bugs.; con: Requires returning `Map<ID, Value>`.
alternatives: name: Lookahead SQL Join Builder; whenToUse: Single-DB GraphQL (e.g., Hasura/PostGraphile).; tradeOff: Cannot span PostgreSQL + gRPC microservices.
failureModes: name: Singleton DataLoader Leak; description: Caching across requests leaks PII.; mitigation: Ensure framework creates a new `DataLoaderRegistry` per HTTP request.

stages.learnerPrompt: Why is `MappedBatchLoader` safer than positional `BatchLoader<K, V>` when calling `Seller-Service`?

referenceMaterial.summary: `BatchLoader` requires the returned `List<V>` to match the exact size and order of `List<K>`, whereas `MappedBatchLoader` keys by ID and safely returns `null` for missing sellers.
approachSteps: Missing/deleted sellers resolve to `null` instead of shifting array indices.
tradeOffs: factor: Map Alignment; pro: Zero index-shift corruption if a seller was deleted.; con: Negligible hash-map allocation.
alternatives: name: Positional List with Null Padding; whenToUse: Legacy DataLoader APIs.; tradeOff: Error-prone if SQL `WHERE id IN (...)` returns fewer rows.
failureModes: name: Size Mismatch Exception; description: DataLoader throws `IllegalStateException` if `result.size() != keys.size()`.; mitigation: Always use `MappedBatchLoader` or pad missing keys.

stages.learnerPrompt: What if a client passes `orders(first: 5000)` to bypass your depth limit of 6?

referenceMaterial.summary: Enforce hard `maxPageSize = 50` in input validation and multiply complexity by `first` (`5000 * 10 = 50,000 > 500`).
approachSteps: Clamp or reject `first > 50` at schema/argument validation.
Use a field-cost calculator that multiplies child cost by `first`.
tradeOffs: factor: Argument Clamping vs. Rejection; pro: Rejecting with `400` forces clients to paginate properly.; con: Breaking change if old clients requested `first: 200`.
alternatives: name: Persisted Query Allowlist; whenToUse: First-party mobile/web apps.; tradeOff: Blocks arbitrary `first` values completely.
failureModes: name: Unweighted Complexity; description: Scoring `orders(first: 5000)` as cost 1 lets giant queries pass.; mitigation: Multiply subtree cost by `first`/`limit`.

stages.learnerPrompt: How do you roll out Persisted Queries without breaking the existing mobile app already in users' hands?

referenceMaterial.summary: Deploy Automatic Persisted Queries (APQ) first, collect all legacy query hashes for 30 days, seed them into the allowlist, then enforce strict allowlist.
approachSteps: Enable APQ (hash -> query cached in Redis).
Log all unpersisted queries from older app versions and add their hashes to the allowlist before flipping `allowArbitraryQueries = false`.
referenceMaterial.codeSnippet:
graphql:
  persistedQueries:
    mode: ALLOWLIST_ONLY
    redisCacheTtlSeconds: 86400
    legacyGracePeriodDays: 30
tradeOffs: factor: Phased Allowlist Enforcement; pro: Zero breakage for older mobile app versions.; con: 30-day transition window before full lockdown.
alternatives: name: Client Version Header Enforcement; whenToUse: When forced-upgrade is supported.; tradeOff: Poor UX if users are forced to update.
failureModes: name: CI Fails to Upload New App Hashes; description: New mobile release fails in production with `PersistedQueryNotFound`.; mitigation: Publish query manifest to S3/Redis as a blocking step in mobile CI before store release.

spark.summary: A single nested GraphQL query (`orders(first: 50) { items { product { seller { rating } } } }`) triggers 1 + 50 + 200 + 200 = 451 sequential DB/gRPC calls per HTTP request, saturating PostgreSQL at just 60 RPS.
spark.keyTakeaway: Always pair request-scoped `DataLoader` batching (collapsing N+1 into `WHERE id IN (...)`) with GraphQL query depth/complexity limits and persisted query allowlists.

Ensure `DataLoader` caches are strictly request-scoped so user A never sees user B's data or stale mutations.

concept.whyItMatters: GraphQL lets clients arbitrarily compose nested graphs, which breaks traditional REST endpoint cost assumptions. Without DataLoader batching, a harmless-looking 3-level query turns into hundreds of sequential round-trips, and without depth/complexity limits, a single 6-level cyclic query can DoS your entire backend.
whenToUse: Request-scoped `DataLoader` on every `@SchemaMapping` / field resolver that fetches related entities by ID.
Query Complexity + Max Depth analysis (`maxDepth = 5`, `maxComplexity = 500`) executed *before* resolver execution.
Automatic Persisted Queries (APQ) or strict Persisted Query Allowlists in production.
whenNotToUse: Never share a global/singleton `DataLoader` across HTTP requests (leaks data between users and caches stale state).
Never run unconstrained `first: 10000` pagination without capping `maxPageSize = 50`.
keyPoints: `DataLoader` collects all keys requested during a single GraphQL execution tick and dispatches one batched `SELECT ... WHERE id = ANY($1)` or `BatchGetSellers(ids)` RPC.
Order matters: `O(levels)` batched queries (4 total) instead of `O(N * M)` (451 total) cuts DB QPS by **>110x**.
Query Complexity scoring assigns higher cost to list multipliers (`orders(first: 50)` multiplies child cost by 50) and rejects queries exceeding budget before execution.
Persisted Query Allowlists eliminate arbitrary ad-hoc queries from public clients.
terms: DataLoader Batching: A per-request utility that coalesces individual `load(id)` calls from sibling resolvers into a single `batchLoad(List<ID>)` call.
Query Complexity Analysis: Static pre-execution AST scoring that multiplies field weights by list `first`/`limit` arguments and rejects queries above a threshold.
Persisted Query Allowlist: A security and performance pattern where clients send a SHA-256 query hash instead of raw GraphQL text, allowing only pre-approved queries in prod.

tradeOffs.pro: Works seamlessly across heterogeneous backends (PostgreSQL + gRPC `Seller-Service`) without coupling schemas.
tradeOffs.con: Executes 1 query per tree depth (4 queries) rather than 1 giant SQL join.

tradeOffs.factor: Persisted Queries vs. Open GraphQL Endpoint
tradeOffs.pro: Eliminates arbitrary DoS queries and shrinks request payload size.
tradeOffs.con: Requires CI step to register client query hashes before app release.

failureModes.name: Cross-Request DataLoader Cache Leak
failureModes.description: Registering DataLoader as a Spring `@Bean` singleton leaks User A's orders to User B.
failureModes.mitigation: Instantiate a fresh `DataLoaderRegistry` per HTTP request (`@RequestScope` / `DgsDataLoader`).

failureModes.name: Cyclic GraphQL Depth Bomb
failureModes.description: Client queries `order -> seller -> orders -> seller ...` 10 levels deep.

commonMistakes: Using `DataLoader` for `product -> seller` but forgetting `order -> items`, leaving an N+1 at level 2.
Forgetting to enforce `maxBatchSize`, causing SQL parameter limit errors (`>65535` in PostgreSQL).
Allowing introspection and arbitrary ad-hoc queries in production without complexity limits.
Not deduping keys inside `batchLoad` (e.g., 200 items from 15 unique sellers should only fetch 15 sellers).

sections.content:
## The Problem

A mobile release added `seller { rating }` to Order History (`orders(first: 50)`). Without batching, field resolvers fire independently: `1 (orders) + 50 (items) + 200 (products) + 200 (sellers) = 451` backend calls per request. At **60 RPS**, PostgreSQL and `Seller-Service` receive **27,060 QPS**, exhausting pools and causing 503s.

## Requirements & Constraints

- **Query Reduction**: Collapse **451** calls down to **<= 4** batched calls.
- **DoS Protection**: Block deep cyclic or high-multiplier queries before execution.
- **Latency**: **<120 ms p99** at **500 RPS**.

## Capacity & Reduction Math

- **Before**: `500 RPS * 451 calls = 225,500 QPS` (impossible).
- **After DataLoader**: `1` Orders query + `1` `WHERE order_id = ANY($1)` Items query + `1` `WHERE id = ANY($1)` Products query + `1` `BatchGetSellers(uniqueIds)` gRPC call = **4 calls/request** (`2,000 QPS` at 500 RPS — a **112x** reduction!).

data.title: GraphQL Complexity Gate + Per-Request DataLoader Batching

edges.label: Validate Depth<=6 & Complexity<=500
edges.title: Pre-Execution AST Guard
edges.description: Rejects cyclic or `first: 5000` queries before any resolver runs.

edges.label: 50x itemsLoader.load(orderId)
edges.title: Coalesce Sibling Resolvers
edges.description: Request-scoped DataLoader buffers all 50 orderIds in one execution tick.

edges.label: 1x WHERE order_id = ANY($1) + 1x products
edges.title: Batched SQL Execution
edges.description: Fetches all 200 items and unique products in 2 single SQL round-trips.

edges.label: 1x BatchGetSellers(uniqueSellerIds)
edges.title: Deduplicated gRPC Batch
edges.description: Deduplicates 200 item references into ~15 unique seller IDs and fetches ratings in 1 RPC.

data.caption: AST complexity guards block abusive queries upfront while request-scoped DataLoaders collapse 451 N+1 calls into 4 batched queries.

sections.content:
## Failure Handling

- **Seller-Service Down**: `SellerDataLoader` catches gRPC failure and returns `rating: null` (nullable schema field) so Order History still renders.
- **Abusive Query**: Complexity > 500 returns HTTP 400 `QUERY_COMPLEXITY_EXCEEDED` in <1 ms without touching PostgreSQL.

## Final Answer

Eliminate the GraphQL N+1 cascade by:
1. **Wiring request-scoped `DataLoader`s** on `items`, `products`, and `sellers` (`451 -> 4` calls).
2. **Enforcing `MaxQueryDepth(6)`, `MaxQueryComplexity(500)`, and `maxPageSize(50)`** before execution.
3. **Moving production mobile clients to a Persisted Query Allowlist**.
